question_text: Long before conversations about glass ceilings and workplace equality became commonplace, CB Muthamma (in picture) was quietly rewriting the rules of ______. Born on 24 January 1924 in Virajpet, Kodagu, she excelled academically and, in 1948, became the first woman to X, subsequently joining the Y in 1949 as its first-ever woman employee. Her pioneering career saw her represent her employer across the world, but her most enduring legacy is from a legal battle against her own employer. Challenging rules that required women officers to seek employer permission before marriage and allowed the employer to compel their resignation after marriage, she approached the Supreme Court in a case that culminated in the landmark judgment C. In a strongly worded opinion, Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer condemned the discriminatory provisions and called upon to purge such misogynistic rules from service. What is X and Y? 5pts each
answer_text: X - first woman to clear UPSC exams. Y - Indian Foreign Services. (The case was C B Muthamma v Union of India, 1979 SCC (4) 260: "We do not mean to universalise or dogmatise that men and women are equal in all occupations and all situations and do not exclude the need to pragmatise where the requirements of particular employment, the sensitivities of sex or the peculiarities of societal sectors or the 672 handicaps of either sex may compel selectivity. But save where the differentiation is demonstrable, the rule of equality must govern.")

question_text: In May 1947, the leaders of Y wrote to X that: "The country is now on the threshold of momentous constitutional change. We did not press for justice so long as everything was in a fluid state. But now it is high time that the authorities should take stock of the situation and mete out even-handed justice. In the future constitution we should be treated as a separate Community, and there must be provisions for separate representation for us in the legislatures ... so that our own culture and tradition may be maintained." The petition came from a community living on a shifting char at the fork of the Padma River in Bengal. The phrase "fluid state" was both political and literal: their land itself frequently moved across district boundaries as the river changed course. Written just weeks before the announcement of Partition, the letter expressed fears about how impending constitutional and territorial changes would affect their identity and representation. Identify X and Y.
answer_text: X = The Constituent Assembly of India. Y = The Moshalchis of Char Balasia.

question_text: X famously stated saying "My first stop on any time-travel expedition would be ____ in December 1947." He chose this specific time and place because December 1947 was when ___ physicists John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley successfully invented the Y, the foundational building block of all modern microchips, computers, and digital technology. X also further stated "Without the invention of the Y, I'm quite sure that the PC would not exist as we know it today." Identify X and Y.

At the turn of the 20th century, the princely state of Mysore embarked on a project that would transform the technological landscape of India. Seeking to power the deep gold mines of Kolar, the Mysore Government selected X, an American start up, to construct a hydroelectric power station at the Shivanasamudra Falls on the Cauvery River. Completed in 1902, the project was among Asia's earliest major hydroelectric achievements. The electricity generated was transmitted over a 147-kilometre (92-mile) line to the Kolar Gold Fields, making it the longest power transmission line in the world at the time. An unintended beneficiary of this venture was Bangalore, which became the first city in India to receive electricity. Identify X.

In the late 1990s and early 2000s, ____ farmers across India were fighting a losing battle against the dreaded American bollworm. To save their crops, many resorted to repeated pesticide spraying. At the same time, a genetically modified technology that could make ___ plants resistant to the bollworm was mired in regulatory delays. Supporters countered that the delays had less to do with science and more to do with the influence of entrenched interests, particularly a powerful pesticide lobby that stood to lose billions if farmers no longer needed frequent spraying. The conflict came to a head in Gujarat in 2001 when farmers planted Navbharat 151, a ___ hybrid that was later found to contain the unapproved Bt gene. The results were dramatic: while neighbouring fields were ravaged by bollworm attacks, these crops flourished. Alarmed by the spread of this "illegal" technology, the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) ordered state authorities to uproot and burn thousands of acres of standing ___ crops, and even destroy the harvested produce. What happened next was one of the most unusual episodes in Indian agricultural history. A farmers' organization, Shetgari Sanghatan launched a Satyagraha in support of them. Its members stood guard in farmers' fields, publicly defied government orders, and warned officials that any attempt to burn crops would be met with mass rural resistance. The movement argued that denying farmers access to a technology that reduced pesticide use, protected yields, and improved incomes amounted to bureaucratic oppression. Their campaign became so successful that enforcement of the burn order became practically impossible, and within a year the technology received official approval. Fill in the blank.

Major Dhyan Chand, the legendary field hockey player, is known for his amazing ball control and goal-scoring skills, along with three Olympic gold medals. When he played for India, the team was at its peak. In the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics, India beat Austria 6-0, Belgium 9-0, Denmark 5-0, and Switzerland 6-0. In the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics, India won against Japan 11-0 and thrashed the USA 24-1, a world record at that time until it was broken in 2003. Dhyan Chand and his brother Roop scored 25 of India's 35 goals. None of these however, was the best match he played according to him. It was his game for his home team, Jhansi Heroes. In 1933, Dhyan Chand's home team, Jhansi Heroes, won the Beighton Cup, against Calcutta Customs. He says that this was the best match he ever played. How many goals did Dhyan Chand score in this game?
answer_text: ZERO. In his own words: "If anybody asked me which was the best match that I played in, I will unhesitatingly say that it was the 1933 Beighton Cup final between Calcutta Customs and Jhansi Heroes... It was a great match, full of thrills, and it was just opportunism that gave us the victory. Customs were pressing hard and our goal was at their mercy. Suddenly I broke through and from midfield gave a long through pass to Ismail, who ran with Jesse Owens' speed half the length of the ground. A misunderstanding occurred between the Customs left-half and the goalkeeper, and Ismail, taking every advantage of it, cut through and netted the only goal of the match. We felt very proud of our triumph." Dhyan Chand himself did not score in this match.

question_text: When discussing longevity on Indian television, names such as Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah, CID, or Kyunki Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi often dominate the conversation. Yet all of them are dwarfed by a programme that predates daily television transmissions in India, predates colour television by 15 years, and has been on air since 26.01.1967. Conceived as a public-service broadcast, it was initially watched in "Teleclubs" across about 80 villages around Delhi, where ____ gathered around community television sets to receive information regarding various aspects of their field work. As India underwent the Green Revolution, economic liberalisation, the satellite-TV boom, and the internet age, this programme quietly continued its mission, eventually moving to a dedicated channel and crossing more than 16,000 episodes. Identify this programme, officially recognized as the longest-running television series in Indian history.

According to a popular legend associated with a famous pilgrimage town on the western coast, the demon-king Ravana performed severe penance to obtain the Atmalinga from Lord Shiva. Shiva granted the boon, but with one condition: the sacred linga would become permanently rooted wherever it first touched the ground. Alarmed that Ravana might become invincible if he carried it successfully to Lanka, the gods sought help from Ganesha. Disguised as a young boy, Ganesha tricked Ravana into handing over the Atmalinga while he performed his evening prayers. The boy then placed it on the ground, where it became immovable. Enraged, Ravana tried to uproot it with immense force, but failed. According to the legend, the shape formed during this struggle resembled a cow's ear, giving the place its name. Identify this town, today revered as the site where the Atmalinga remains enshrined.

"Congratulations, you are now officially one of the most wanted men in England." This line comes from a 2005 cult film that follows Matt Buckner, an American journalism student who, after being expelled from Harvard, travels to London and is drawn into the violent and fiercely loyal world of English football hooligan firms. The film revolves around the fictional _____, a group of supporters whose code of honour, territorial rivalries, and organised clashes with rival firms drive the story. Although fictional, the ___ is widely regarded as being inspired by the Inter City Firm (ICF), one of the most infamous hooligan groups in British football history. Active primarily during the 1970s and 1980s, the ICF took its name from the InterCity trains its members used to travel to away matches. Another clue lies in the recurring use of the anthem "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles," long associated with the club whose supporters formed the ICF. Name both the film (5pts) and the football club (5pts) that inspired its central hooligan firm.
answer_text: Green Street Hooligans (or Green Street in the UK). West Ham United F.C.

question_text: In the decades after World War II, the U.S. Army faced an unusual problem: soldiers were being given nutritionally adequate field rations, but many simply refused to eat enough of them. To solve this, the Army's Natick Laboratories began studying food preference scientifically, treating taste not as an art but as a measurable engineering problem. One of the researchers involved was a Harvard-trained psychophysicist named Howard Moskowitz who analysed how people responded to flavour, texture, sweetness, saltiness, and variety. His military research helped develop systematic methods for measuring food acceptance, preference scales, and sensory response. The underlying idea was that a food could be mathematically optimized so that people would consume more of it. After leaving the Army, Howard Moskowitz applied the same principles to consumer products, helping companies such as Campbell's, PepsiCo, Kraft, and Prego design foods tailored to different preference groups. His work eventually popularised a concept known as the "______" and consumer segmentation, becoming foundational to what is now known as food engineering and sensory science which eventually led to the making of the Ultra-processed foods. Fill in the blank. (10pts)

A cricket scorecard is shown for India's innings (50 overs maximum): Virender Sehwag 130, Sachin Tendulkar 102, Sourav Ganguly (c) 33, Yuvraj Singh 7, and a batter whose name is masked out who scored 50 not out off 22 balls with 5 fours and 3 sixes (strike rate 227.27). Identify the Indian batter whose name is masked (5pts) and the venue where this game was held (5pts).
answer_text: Rahul Dravid. Lal Bahadur Shastri Stadium, Hyderabad.

question_text: In April 1819, a young officer of the 28th Cavalry of the British East India Company was on a tiger-hunting expedition in the rugged forests of the ___ when he noticed what appeared to be an arch-shaped facade hidden behind thick vegetation on a cliff face overlooking the Waghora River. Pushing through the undergrowth, he and his companions found themselves standing before a vast complex of rock-cut Buddhist monasteries and prayer halls that had lain forgotten for centuries. The discovery would eventually lead to the global recognition of one of India's greatest artistic and archaeological treasures, famed for its exquisite murals, sculptures, and architecture dating from the 2nd century BCE to the 6th century CE. Yet the officer's own contribution to the site remains controversial. Eager to commemorate his "discovery," he carved his name, rank, and the date - "28 April 1819" - onto a pillar inside Cave 10, leaving behind what is perhaps the most famous act of colonial-era graffiti in India. Remarkably, the inscription survives to this day and can still be seen by visitors. Identify both the officer (5pts) and the archaeological site (5pts) associated with this infamous inscription.
Connect: 1. John Milton, 2. Charles Darwin, 3. Jane Goodall, 4. Alan Turing, 5. E.M. Forster, 6. Stephen Hawking, 7. The King of Jordan, 8. Subhash Chandra Bose.
answer_text: All of them studied at Cambridge University.

question_text: A former performance coach, X, who has worked with many successful sports teams, once drew an unexpected comparison between two national teams. He argued that Y team's players were so well physically conditioned that, were a squad from the Z team asked to complete even half of their routine training session, most would be unable to finish. The coach identified only one contemporary athlete as having a realistic chance of keeping pace. He then delivered a memorable line, describing the members of the Y squad as essentially being 18 versions of that athlete from a fitness standpoint. Identify X (4), Y (3) and Z (3).
answer_text: X: Paddy Upton. Y: Indian Hockey Team. Z: Indian Cricket Team.

question_text: In 1877, X and her colleague Charles Bradlaugh republished The Fruits of Philosophy, a pamphlet written by American physician Charles Knowlton. The pamphlet explained contraception and argued that poor families should be able to control the number of children they had. At the time, information about birth control was widely considered obscene. X and Bradlaugh deliberately republished the work to test Britain's obscenity laws and the limits of free discussion on contraception. They even informed the authorities that they were selling the pamphlet. The Crown charged them with publishing an obscene libel under Victorian obscenity laws. The prosecution argued that the book was likely to "corrupt public morals" and encourage sexual immorality. The jury initially returned a guilty verdict. The trial judge imposed fines and prison sentences, though execution of the sentence was suspended pending appeal. However, the conviction was later set aside on a technical defect in the indictment. As a result, X and Bradlaugh avoided imprisonment and the prosecution ultimately failed. The case became a cause celebre across Britain. Ironically, the prosecution made the pamphlet vastly more popular, turning it into a bestseller and bringing public discussion of birth control into the mainstream. Historians often regard the Knowlton Trial as a foundational moment in the British birth control movement and in the struggle for freedom of expression. ID X, who is popular in India also for other reasons.

This mythological anti-hero (X) has always been seen as a treacherous villain in the ___ War. For many, the mere name 'X' provokes a thought of evil and deceit. Yet his name has always meant a warrior who is difficult to defeat or someone who is extremely difficult to fight or wage war against. Despite his wrong doings, he was considered by many scholars as a fair king, a brilliant strategist and a dutiful Kshatriya. There are villages in Uttarakhand where X has been worshiped as a deity. A X temple in Jakhol village in Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand was built by the inhabitants of Saur, who worship ______ as their ancestors. Other temples dedicated to the antihero can be seen at Osla, Kotegoan and Datmir. Further, there is a temple dedicated to X down south in Kerala known as the Malanada Temple, also known as the Poruvazhy Peruvathy Malanada Temple. Local tradition says that during his search for his enemies, X passed through the region, was given water by a woman from a marginalized community, and, in gratitude, granted land and privileges to the local people. As a result, the local community remembers him not as a villain but as a generous and just ruler. ID X.

Decades before the Revolt of 1857 and more than a century before revolutionary figures such as Bhagat Singh entered the national imagination, a woman commander in southern India carried out one of the most audacious attacks against the British East India Company. Serving as the Commander-in-Chief of the all-women Udayal Padai under Velu Nachiyar, she devised a plan to destroy a heavily guarded British ammunition depot during the Vijayadashami festivities. After covering herself in ghee and oil collected from temple lamps, she set herself ablaze and rushed into the armoury, triggering an explosion that crippled the British garrison and helped her queen reclaim the kingdom of Sivagangai in 1780. Remembered in Tamil folklore as Theepaanchi Amman and often described as India's first female suicide attacker against colonial forces, who was this warrior?
